text: "Return to the stronghold, you prisoners of hope. Even today I declare that I will restore double to you."
explanation:
Many of us used to be prisoners of hopelessness: lying awake, unable to escape dark thoughts no matter how hard we tried to look on the bright side. God doesn't just release you from that prison. He makes you a prisoner of hope, so hopeful you can't help it, even when you try to think the worst.

And it rests on something solid: "Because of the blood of your covenant, I will set your prisoners free." The world says, "Don't raise your hopes." But your God is the God of hope, and your hope is anchored in the blood of Jesus. Expect double.

text: The first time the Hebrew word tikvah (hope) appears, it means a rope: the scarlet cord Rahab hung from her window.
explanation:
Rahab hid Israel's two spies and let them down from her window in Jericho's wall. They told her, "Bind this line of scarlet cord in the window… and bring your father, your mother, your brothers and all your father's household into your home." The word for cord is tikvah, the same word as hope; Israel's national anthem is called Hatikvah, "The Hope."

Hope is a rope let down to someone in a pit. And Rahab's was scarlet, the colour of blood. Your hope isn't wishful thinking. It's tied to the blood of Jesus, and it's strong enough to save your whole household.

text: From her window Rahab saw only destruction coming. God saw the great-great-grandmother of King David, and an ancestor of the Messiah.
explanation:
Rahab had no future in Jericho, and a prostitute had no obvious place in Israel. All she had was a promise and a scarlet cord. When the walls of Jericho fell flat, her family was spared. She married Salmon of the tribe of Judah and became the mother of Boaz, who married Ruth. Their great-grandson was David, and her name stands in the genealogy of Jesus Christ.

The same window that showed only doom became the window of her deliverance. However bleak your view looks right now, God sees much further down the line than you do.

text: "The Lord is God of the hills, but He is not God of the valleys," said the Syrians. God answered by defeating them in the valley.
explanation:
After Israel defeated a vast Syrian army in the hills, the Syrians decided Israel's God only had power up there. Next time they would fight on the plain. God sent word: "Because the Syrians have said, 'The Lord is God of the hills, but He is not God of the valleys,' therefore I will deliver all this great multitude into your hand, and you shall know that I am the Lord." Israel camped "like two little flocks of goats," and the enemy was routed.

The enemy wants you to believe God is only with you on the mountaintops, when you're doing well. Jesus came down from the Mount of Transfiguration to deliver a tormented boy in the valley. He's God of your valley too.

text: Psalm 23 says "He leads me" until the valley. Then it changes to "You are with me." In the valley, talk to Him, not just about Him.
explanation:
"The Lord is my shepherd… He makes me lie down… He leads me…" David is talking about the Lord in the third person, as we often do with friends. But when he reaches "the valley of the shadow of death," he switches: "I will fear no evil, for You are with me; Your rod and Your staff, they comfort me. You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies."

Notice too: you walk through the valley. You don't camp there. And the table is set in the presence of your enemies, not after they've gone. In your trial, don't just talk about God; talk to Him.

text: Muse means to meditate. Put an "a" in front and you get amuse: no meditation. We live in an age of amusement.
explanation:
"While I was musing, the fire burned," said David. To muse is to turn something over and over in your mind, to meditate. The prefix "a" negates it. A generation filled with amusement has very little time left to muse.

Try it with words you've known for years. "The Lord is my shepherd." Who is? The Lord, not the richest person in the world. Is: past, present and future. My: personally mine. Shepherd: feeding, guiding, protecting. Put the phone down now and then and let the Word sink in. That's where the fire starts.

text: Jacob said, "All these things are against me." In fact, every one of them was working for him.
explanation:
Jacob thought Joseph was dead and Simeon was gone, and now the Egyptian governor was demanding Benjamin. "All these things are against me," he groaned. He didn't know the governor was Joseph, alive and ruling Egypt, asking about his father and longing to see his brother.

"We know that all things work together for good to those who love God." The Greek is synergeo, a synergy. The delay, the red light, the closed door may be part of His plan for you. Things may look against you, but if you belong to God, they're working for you.
